title: Hepatitis B Serology: Markers, Timeline and the Window Period
summary: Meet the four hepatitis B markers, watch them rise and fall on a timeline, find the window where HBsAg and anti-HBs are both negative, and read a panel like a lab scientist.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 22 Hit 1 (core: hepatitis B core window), the HBV part of Hit 10 (chronicity by age, with CDC figures) and the Figure 22 memory anchor. HCV chronicity (Hit 10) is not taught. See register flags rv-hbv-chronicity and rv-hbv-window-sole.

objectives: State what HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc and IgM anti-HBc each indicate.
Place the markers on the timeline of acute and chronic infection and identify the window period.
Interpret common serology patterns, including vaccination and isolated anti-HBc, and the effect of age on chronicity.

scenes.title: Negative and negative
scenes.altText: A patient recovering from an acute hepatitis-like illness. The lab card shows HBsAg negative and anti-HBs negative. A tempting conclusion token — “Never had hepatitis B” — appears, then wobbles with a question mark. One more test card waits face-down.

cues.text: A patient is recovering from an illness that looked like acute hepatitis. HBsAg is negative. Anti-HBs is negative too.
It’s tempting to say: never had hepatitis B. But that can be wrong.
There is a stretch of time when both of these are negative in someone who is infected. One more test catches it.

scenes.title: Normal: what each marker means
scenes.altText: Four marker cards. HBsAg (surface antigen): present during acute or chronic infection; the first serologic marker, usually within 1–10 weeks. Anti-HBs: recovery and immunity, and the only marker after vaccination. Total anti-HBc: contact with the virus at some time (not produced by vaccination). IgM anti-HBc: recent infection, within about 6 months.

cues.text: HBsAg, the surface antigen, means the virus is there now — in acute or chronic infection. It is usually the first serologic marker, appearing within about 1 to 10 weeks.
Anti-HBs, antibody to the surface antigen, means recovery and immunity. After vaccination it is the only marker you see.
Total anti-HBc, antibody to the core, means the person has met the virus at some time. Vaccines don’t make it.
IgM anti-HBc means recent infection — usually within the last six months. It marks acute hepatitis B.

props.title: Total anti-HBc
lines: Met the virus at some time

scenes.title: What changes: the timeline and the window
scenes.altText: A schematic timeline from infection to about a year. Acute resolving infection: an HBsAg bar rises and ends before 6 months; an IgM anti-HBc bar starts soon after and fades within about 6 months; a total anti-HBc bar starts and runs to the end; an anti-HBs bar starts only after HBsAg has gone. The gap between the end of HBsAg and the start of anti-HBs is shaded and labelled “window”: HBsAg and anti-HBs both negative, while anti-HBc (including IgM) is positive and HBV DNA may be detectable. Then the chronic version: HBsAg runs past the 6-month line and anti-HBs never appears.

cues.text: Here is a schematic timeline of acute hepatitis B that resolves. HBsAg appears first, then fades as the body clears the virus.
Anti-core antibodies appear soon after: IgM first, fading within about six months, and total anti-HBc that stays for life.
Anti-HBs appears only after HBsAg is gone. The gap between them is the window: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative — but anti-HBc, including IgM, is positive, and HBV DNA may be detectable.
In chronic infection, HBsAg is still there after six months, and anti-HBs never appears. HBsAg lasting six months or more defines chronic hepatitis B.

scenes.title: In the lab: reading the panel
scenes.altText: A results table builds row by row (HBsAg / total anti-HBc / IgM anti-HBc / anti-HBs): + + + − acute infection; + + − − chronic infection; − + (IgM ±) ± resolving or resolved infection; − − − + immune from vaccination; − − − − susceptible. A last row, isolated total anti-HBc (− + − −), lists possibilities: resolved infection with waned anti-HBs, occult infection, passive transfer to an infant, false positive, or a mutant strain. A note: adults are screened with the triple panel (HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc).

cues.text: Labs read the markers together. Surface antigen, core antibody and IgM core antibody positive, surface antibody negative: acute infection.
Surface antigen and core antibody positive, but IgM negative and no surface antibody: chronic infection.
Surface antigen gone, core antibody positive, surface antibody positive: resolved infection. Only surface antibody: immunity from vaccination. All negative: susceptible.
Core antibody alone is the puzzle: resolved infection with faded anti-HBs, occult infection, antibody passed to an infant, a false positive, or a mutant strain.
That’s why adults are screened with a triple panel: HBsAg, anti-HBs and total anti-HBc.

props.label: HBsAg · total anti-HBc · IgM anti-HBc · anti-HBs
Adults: triple panel — HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc

scenes.title: Two traps and one age rule
scenes.altText: Trap card: “HBsAg − and anti-HBs − = never infected” is crossed out → “Check (IgM) anti-HBc: the window period.” Trap card: “Anti-HBs + = past infection” is crossed out → “Anti-HBs alone (anti-HBc −) = vaccination.” Then an age bar: chance of chronic infection about 90% for infected infants, about 30% at ages 1–5, and about 5% in adults.

cues.text: Trap one: HBsAg and anti-HBs both negative doesn’t prove someone was never infected. Check anti-HBc — especially IgM — to catch the window period.
Trap two: anti-HBs positive doesn’t always mean past infection. If anti-HBc is negative, the immunity came from vaccination.
And age decides the outcome. About 90 percent of infected infants stay chronically infected, about 30 percent of children aged one to five, and only about 5 percent of adults.

props.title: ✗ “HBsAg − and anti-HBs − = never infected.”
lines: ✓ Check anti-HBc / IgM anti-HBc — the window

scenes.title: Sick, Safe, Contact, Current
scenes.altText: Memory aid: four badges. S-antigen = Sick now. Anti-S = Safe (immune). Anti-core = Contact (met the virus). IgM anti-core = Current (recent). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: surface antigen means Sick now. Anti-surface means Safe. Anti-core means Contact — you met the virus. IgM anti-core means Current — it was recent.

Where it breaks: occult infection can hide behind negative HBsAg, mutant strains and false positives exist, IgM anti-HBc can reappear at low level during flares of chronic hepatitis B, and timing varies between people.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “HBsAg sick · anti-HBs safe · anti-HBc contact · IgM recent”, “Window: HBsAg − and anti-HBs − → test (IgM) anti-HBc”, “HBsAg ≥ 6 months = chronic · age decides (≈90% infants vs ≈5% adults)”.

cues.text: In hepatitis B, HBsAg means current infection, anti-HBs means immunity and anti-HBc means past contact, so when HBsAg and anti-HBs are both negative after illness, test IgM anti-HBc to catch the window period.

props.label: HBsAg sick · anti-HBs safe · anti-HBc contact · IgM recent
Window: HBsAg − and anti-HBs − → test (IgM) anti-HBc

explanation.what: Plain language: hepatitis B tests look for a piece of the virus (surface antigen) and the body’s antibodies to two parts of it (surface and core). Scientific terms: HBsAg indicates current infection; anti-HBs indicates recovery or vaccine immunity; total anti-HBc indicates infection at some time; IgM anti-HBc indicates recent (acute) infection, usually within 6 months.
explanation.why: After infection HBsAg appears first (usually within 1–10 weeks). If the infection resolves, HBsAg clears and anti-HBs appears later; in the gap (window) only anti-HBc — including IgM — is positive and HBV DNA may be detectable. HBsAg persisting ≥ 6 months defines chronic infection. Age at infection determines chronicity: about 90% of infected infants, 30% of children aged 1–5 and about 5% of adults.
explanation.measure: Serology panel: HBsAg, total anti-HBc, IgM anti-HBc, anti-HBs; adults are screened with the triple panel (HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc). HBV DNA (NAT) detects virus in the window and in occult infection.
explanation.differs: Vaccine immunity (anti-HBs only) vs natural immunity (anti-HBs + anti-HBc); acute (IgM anti-HBc +) vs chronic (HBsAg ≥ 6 months, IgM usually −); window (HBsAg −, anti-HBs −, anti-HBc +) vs susceptible (all negative).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: “HBsAg and anti-HBs negative — what next?” (IgM anti-HBc), vaccinated vs recovered patterns, acute vs chronic, isolated anti-HBc possibilities, and age-dependent chronicity.

questions.stem: Three weeks after an acute hepatitis illness, a patient has negative HBsAg and negative anti-HBs. Which test best identifies recent hepatitis B infection now?

options.rationale: Correct. In the window between HBsAg clearance and anti-HBs appearance, anti-HBc — including IgM — is positive and marks recent infection.
Incorrect. That would delay the diagnosis; IgM anti-HBc answers the question now.
Incorrect. Anti-HCV tests for hepatitis C, not hepatitis B.

options.text: Conclude the patient was never infected
options.rationale: Incorrect. Both markers are negative during the window period of a resolving infection.

questions.stem: A health-care worker has HBsAg −, total anti-HBc −, anti-HBs + (120 mIU/mL). What is the interpretation?

options.rationale: Correct. Anti-HBs alone, with negative anti-HBc, indicates vaccine-induced immunity.
Incorrect. Natural infection would also leave anti-HBc positive.
Incorrect. Chronic infection requires HBsAg positivity.
Incorrect. The window has anti-HBc positive and anti-HBs negative.

questions.stem: A patient’s HBsAg has remained positive for 8 months; IgM anti-HBc is negative and anti-HBs is negative. What is the interpretation?

options.rationale: Correct. HBsAg persisting 6 months or longer defines chronic infection.
Incorrect. Acute infection shows IgM anti-HBc, and HBsAg usually clears within 6 months if it resolves.
Incorrect. Resolution means HBsAg is negative and anti-HBs positive.
Incorrect. Vaccines produce anti-HBs, not HBsAg persisting for months.

claims.text: HBsAg current infection; anti-HBs immunity (only marker after vaccination); total anti-HBc infection at some time; IgM anti-HBc recent (< 6 months).
In the window (HBsAg −, anti-HBs −), anti-HBc including IgM is positive and HBV DNA may be detectable.
HBsAg first appears within 1–10 weeks; HBsAg ≥ 6 months defines chronic infection.
Interpretation patterns, including isolated anti-HBc possibilities; adult triple-panel screening.
HCV becomes chronic in 75–85%; ~20% of acute cases are jaundiced.
claims.note: Not taught. CDC (2025) says “more than half” develop chronic infection.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer gives HBV chronicity as 80% in neonates and 1–2% in adolescents/adults; CDC gives ~90% of infants, 30% at 1–5 years and ~5% of adults. The lesson teaches the CDC figures.
The reviewer calls IgM anti-HBc the “sole marker” of the window; total anti-HBc (which includes IgM) is also positive and HBV DNA may be detectable. The lesson says “anti-HBc, including IgM”.
Ch. 22 Hit 10 also covers HCV chronicity, which is not taught here.
